claims.l02: Paper p.2 contributions and sec 3.3: every task is authored from scratch and never merged upstream.
claims.l03: Paper abstract and sec 1: most public agentic coding benchmarks follow SWE-bench in mining merged fixes; the fixes are public and 'plausibly in pretraining data, so a high score can reflect recall rather than problem-solving'. Receipt: p.1.
claims.l04: Paper sec 1: inherited tests 'were written to confirm one particular fix, not to grade an arbitrary new solution, so they can reject a valid alternative implementation or accept an incomplete one'. Receipt: p.2.
claims.l05: Paper abstract, sec 3.2: 113 tasks, 91 repositories, five languages (TypeScript, Go, Python, JavaScript, Rust). Receipt: abstract p.1.
claims.l06: Paper sec 5.2 and sec 3.3: one fixed harness (mini-swe-agent, single bash tool, shared prompt); the container ships only a shallow clone at the base commit. Prompts are about half the length of SWE-Bench Pro's.
claims.l07: Paper sec 3.4 and 4.2: hand-written verifiers check the requested functionality and accept any implementation that provides it; regression checks run on every trial and a patch that breaks unrelated functionality fails (p.9).
claims.l08a: Paper abstract and sec 3.4: an independent LLM judge re-reviews graded runs.
claims.l08b: Paper abstract, sec 3.4, sec 8: disagreement rate (not an error rate), small audit, judge GPT-5.5 is also the paper's top configuration. Receipt: abstract p.1 '(1.4% versus 32.4%)'.
claims.l09: Board v1.1: three setups at 74% with overlapping run intervals; average cost per task $2.36, $4.43, $11.84, drawn as coin stacks with no figures.
claims.l10: Paper sec 1 scope and sec 8 limitations: long-horizon multi-file work from a specified prompt; binary pass/fail, no partial credit; code quality not graded; under-specified requests not measured. Receipt: p.3 'not a global ranking of coding products or of overall model quality'.
claims.l11: Paper sec 3.4 opening sentence: 'A benchmark is only as good as its verifier.' Receipt: p.7.
